plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 1.1.7
plan.contextChunk: This figure contains three panels, (a), (b), and (c), illustrating the approximation of the area under a curve by inscribed rectangles. Panel (a): a smooth curve over the interval [a, b] with the entire region between the curve and the x-axis shaded. Panel (b): the same curve with a small number of wide rectangles inscribed under it, giving a coarse Riemann sum approximation. Panel (c): the same curve with many narrow rectangles filling most of the gap, giving a much closer approximation to the true area. The figure introduces the Riemann sum approach to defining the definite integral as the limit of rectangular area approximations as the number of rectangles increases without bound.

interactionPlan.concept: The exact area under a curve on [a, b] is the limit of the sum of inscribed rectangle areas as the number of rectangles n grows without bound — the three textbook panels are just snapshots of that single limiting process.

y-axis with arrowhead and label y
smooth blue curve over [a, b]: low near a, rising to a rounded peak left-of-center, dipping to a trough right-of-center, rising again toward b
vertical segment at x = a from axis to curve
vertical segment at x = b from axis to curve
light-blue shaded region between the curve and the x-axis over [a, b] (the exact area, panel a)
inscribed rectangles under the curve (panels b and c), light-blue fill with thin dark outlines
tick labels 'a' and 'b' on the x-axis
panel captions '(a)', '(b)', '(c)' beneath each panel
numeric readout showing the current Riemann sum value (single view)
annotation showing the exact area value for comparison (single view)

demo_steps.title: The exact area we want
demo_steps.narration: Panel (a) shades the true region between the curve and the x-axis on [a, b]. This exact area is the quantity the rest of the figure works toward approximating.

demo_steps.title: A coarse Riemann sum
demo_steps.narration: Panel (b) replaces the smooth region with a few wide inscribed rectangles. Their total area is only a rough approximation — large gaps remain between the rectangle tops and the curve.

demo_steps.title: Unify into one view
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the single view and use the slider: at small n you recover panel (b)'s coarse bars, and the running sum is shown beside the exact area for comparison.

demo_steps.title: Refine to the limit
demo_steps.narration: Drag n upward: the bars narrow, the gaps vanish, and the running Riemann sum approaches the exact shaded area — illustrating the integral as the limit of these sums as n grows without bound.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The definite integral (area under a curve) is not a new object but the limit of an ordinary sum of rectangle areas as the rectangles become infinitely many and infinitely thin.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use one smooth blue curve (stroke ~3px, color a medium cyan-blue) shaped like a gentle wave: start low just right of the y-axis, climb to a rounded maximum around the left third, descend to a shallow minimum around the right third, then rise again at b. Fill the region under it with a pale translucent blue. In 'Three panels' mode render three side-by-side copies labeled (a), (b), (c): (a) full shaded region with vertical edge lines at a and b; (b) ~6 wide inscribed rectangles; (c) ~20+ narrow rectangles nearly filling the region. In 'Single view' mode render one panel whose rectangle count is driven by nSlider, using left-endpoint heights so bars sit under the curve on rising sections and slightly over on falling sections; show a live numeric Riemann-sum readout and the exact area value as text annotations near the top. Axes are simple black arrows with italic x, y labels and italic a, b ticks. Cross-fade between layouts on toggle rather than an abrupt swap.

authoredPrompt: This figure contains three panels, (a), (b), and (c), illustrating the approximation of the area under a curve by inscribed rectangles. Panel (a): a smooth curve over the interval [a, b] with the entire region between the curve and the x-axis shaded. Panel (b): the same curve with a small number of wide rectangles inscribed under it, giving a coarse Riemann sum approximation. Panel (c): the same curve with many narrow rectangles filling most of the gap, giving a much closer approximation to the true area. The figure introduces the Riemann sum approach to defining the definite integral as the limit of rectangular area approximations as the number of rectangles increases without bound.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for number of rectangles n: watch the bars refine from coarse (panel b) to fine (panel c) and display the running Riemann sum value
- Toggle the three panels into a single animated view to eliminate side-by-side comparison
authoredContext: However, for regions with curved boundaries, such as that in Figure 1.1.7a, a more general approach is needed. One such approach is to begin by approximating the area of the region by inscribing a number of rectangles of equal width under the curve and adding the areas of these rectangles (Figure 1.1.7b). Intuition suggests that if we repeat that approximation process using more and more rectangles, then the rectangles will tend to fill in the gaps under the curve, and the approximations will get closer and closer to the exact area under the curve (Figure 1.1.7c). This suggests that we can define the area under the curve to be the limiting value of these approximations. This idea will be considered in detail later, but the point to note here is that once again the concept of a limit comes into play.

discrepancies: The three panels are drawn nearly square (375x370 each) inside a 1200x470 viewbox, so the rendered figure leaves a large empty band below the panels; the source is a clean wide, low 3-panel strip with no dead whitespace.
The italic tick labels 'a' and 'b' and the axis letters 'x','y' are noticeably smaller relative to panel size than the large prominent italic labels in the source.
In the source the curve stroke is bold and dominant; here the curve (width 3) reads slightly thin against the rectangle edges at small render size.

Panel (c) in the source uses a fixed dense set of thin bars, which is matched, but the slider that changes n only affects the hidden single-view, so the default three-panel view offers no live refinement of panels (b)/(c).
evaluation.notes: The three-panel Riemann-sum-to-integral composition is faithfully reproduced (exact shaded region, 6 left-endpoint bars, ~22 thin bars, correct curve shape, light-blue fill and blue curve), and the single-view toggle plus n-slider with a live running-sum-vs-exact readout and a 4-step demo player are genuinely pedagogical; main weaknesses are the square panel aspect leaving large blank whitespace and undersized a/b/x/y labels versus the source's wide strip and bold italic labels.
action_items: Rescale the layout to a wide, low aspect (e.g. viewbox ~1200x300 with panel height ~230) so the three panels fill the frame like the source and the empty band below disappears.
Increase the font sizes of the 'a','b' tick labels and the italic 'x','y' axis letters (and the (a)/(b)/(c) captions) so they match the source's prominent label hierarchy at inline size.
Thicken the curve stroke slightly (e.g. width 3.5-4) so it stays visually dominant over the rectangle edges.
Optionally let the n-slider also drive panel (b)/(c) density (or label which panel the slider controls) so the default three-panel view participates in the refinement interaction.

feedback.rationale: Concept and interactivity are strong (scores 4–5, no failure modes), but concrete execution issues — wrong aspect ratio leaving dead whitespace, undersized labels, and thin curve stroke — are all generator-level fixes that would improve faithfulness to the source's wide-strip layout.
